# Esther Chapter 1 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 456r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_001_page_001.jpg

---

**1:1** This is what happened during the reign of King Ahasuerus — the very one who ruled over a hundred and twenty-seven provinces stretching from India all the way to Ethiopia.

**1:2** At that time, King Ahasuerus was ruling from his throne in the fortified palace of Susa.

**1:3** In his third year as king, he threw a lavish banquet for all his officials and ministers. The entire military leadership of Persia and Media was there, along with the nobles and provincial governors,

**1:4** and for a full six months — one hundred and eighty days — he put the staggering wealth and splendor of his kingdom on display for all to see.

**1:5** When those days were over, the king held another feast, this one lasting seven days, for everyone living in the citadel of Susa, from the most powerful to the most humble. It was held in the courtyard garden of the royal palace.

**1:6** The courtyard was draped with white and blue-violet linen curtains, tied with cords of fine purple fabric to silver rings on marble columns. Gold and silver couches were arranged on a mosaic floor made of precious stones — alabaster, marble, mother-of-pearl, and dark marble.

**1:7** Wine was served in an assortment of unique golden goblets, and the royal wine flowed freely — as generous as the king himself.

**1:8** By the king's own order, no one was pressured to drink; every server was instructed to let each guest have as much or as little as he wished.

**1:9** Meanwhile, Queen Vashti was hosting her own banquet for the women inside the royal palace.

**1:10** On the seventh day of the feast, when the king was feeling the full effects of the wine, he ordered his seven personal attendants — Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas —

**1:11** to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing the royal crown, so he could show off her beauty to the guests and dignitaries. She was, after all, stunningly beautiful.

**1:12** But Queen Vashti refused to come. The king was humiliated and enraged.

**1:13** He turned to his advisors — men who were experts in law and custom, as was his habit —

**1:14** particularly the seven highest-ranking officials of Persia and Media who had direct access to the king: Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan.

**1:15** "What does the law say should be done to Queen Vashti?" the king demanded. "She has defied a direct order from me, delivered by my own attendants."

**1:16** Memucan spoke up before the king and the entire assembly: "Your Majesty, Queen Vashti has not wronged you alone — she has wronged every official and every citizen across your empire.

**1:17** When word of this gets out — and it will — every woman in the kingdom will feel entitled to disrespect her husband. They will say, 'If Queen Vashti can refuse the king, why should I obey my husband?'

**1:18** Before this day is over, the noblewomen of Persia and Media will be talking about it, and they will use this as an excuse. There will be no end to the disrespect and arguing.

**1:19** If it pleases Your Majesty, issue a royal decree — and have it written permanently into Persian and Median law, so it can never be overturned — that Vashti is permanently banished from your presence, and that her royal position be given to someone more deserving.

**1:20** When this decree is announced throughout your vast empire, every wife will treat her husband with proper respect, regardless of rank."

**1:21** The king and his officials thought this was excellent advice, and the king did exactly as Memucan proposed.

**1:22** He dispatched letters to every province in the empire, written in each region's own script and language, proclaiming that every man should be the master of his own household.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

1. **A Book Without God's Name:** Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible in which God is never mentioned — not by name, not by title, not even indirectly. Yet the entire narrative pulses with the unmistakable rhythms of divine providence. The story invites readers to see God at work precisely where God seems absent — a profound theological statement about hidden faithfulness.

2. **Power, Spectacle, and Fragility:** Chapter 1 is a masterclass in narrative irony. The king who commands 127 provinces cannot command his own wife. Six months of displaying imperial glory dissolves into domestic humiliation. The storyteller signals from the outset that human power — no matter how vast — is fragile and often foolish.

3. **Vashti's Refusal:** The text gives no reason for Vashti's refusal and passes no moral judgment on it. Whether her act was one of dignity or defiance, the narrator leaves readers to decide. What matters for the story is the cascade of consequences her "no" sets in motion — consequences that will ultimately bring Esther to the throne.

*— PNEUMA*
